kurz: Valuation errors almost always arise in the assumptions and hardly ever in the arithmetic; they recur, and they all push the value in the same direction.

bloecke.md:
Investors who already find a share attractive before doing the calculation also discover reasons for a higher value. Each of these reasons is defensible on its own, for example half a percentage point less cost of capital, one percentage point more perpetual growth, or a good year instead of an average one as the starting point. Together, in the following model, they raise the value per share by 69% if the good year is 25% above average. If reinvestment is not adjusted to the higher growth, the figure is 92%. The following errors are therefore ordered by their leverage on the result.

All errors are worked through using a model company. Its figures are model assumptions, not observations: operating profit after tax (NOPAT) of €100 million in the first year, a return on capital ([[Return on invested capital (ROIC)|ROIC]]) of 12%, a [[Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)|WACC]] of 8.5% (the average for mainly German companies in the KPMG cost of capital study 2025) and perpetual growth of 1.5%. The relationship g = ROIC × reinvestment rate gives a reinvestment rate of 12.5% and therefore a free cash flow of €87.5 million. The [[Enterprise value|enterprise value]] is 87.5 / (0.085 − 0.015) = €1,250 million.

bloecke.titel: From enterprise value to value per share (illustrative calculation, €m)
zeilen: = Equity value with 113.1 million diluted shares after five years

bloecke.md:
## Leverage effect of the bridge

The bridge between enterprise value and equity value consists of fixed euro amounts, whereas the enterprise value is a multiple of estimated quantities. Every percentage error in the enterprise value is therefore amplified in the equity value. The leverage is 1,250 divided by 800, which is 1.56. An enterprise value that is 20% too high thus leads to an equity value that is 31% too high.

If the bridge is skipped altogether and the enterprise value is divided directly by the number of shares, the result is €12.50 instead of €8.00 per share. The error becomes particularly large when pension obligations are high. Their value under the HGB (Commercial Code), based on the ten-year average interest rate under Section 253(2) HGB, and their IFRS value, based on the reporting-date rate under IAS 19, differ considerably. Which of the two values belongs in the bridge must be a deliberate decision.

bloecke.titel: Overstatement of the value per share caused by seven errors in the same model company (as a percentage)
bloecke.unter: Each bar shows the percentage by which a single error raises the correctly calculated result. The reference value is €8.00 per share, for dilution €7.07 after five years, and for the tax shield around €7.89 with the add-back.
kategorien: Enterprise value divided directly by the share count

bloecke.md:
## Tax shield and WACC range

The last bar in the chart is the most instructive. It concerns the tax shield, which in Germany is smaller than the formula assumes. For trade tax (Gewerbesteuer), a quarter of financing costs is added back to the extent that they exceed €200,000 (Section 8 no. 1 GewStG, Trade Tax Act). The total burden of around 33% consists of corporation tax of 15%, which comes to 15.825% including the solidarity surcharge, and trade tax of around 17%. Because of the add-back, deducting interest saves only about 28.7% of the interest in tax instead of 33%. In the model, this raises the WACC by 0.06 percentage points and lowers the value by 1.3%.

At the same time, the same valuation depends heavily on the WACC, which reputable valuation reports set within a range of around two percentage points. At 7.5%, the model gives €10.08 per share; at 9.5%, €6.44. If a valuation accounts for the add-back to the cent but conceals the range, it is precise about a quantity that changes the value by 1% and leaves open a quantity that changes it by 57%. With high debt, the interest barrier (Zinsschranke) also applies (Section 4h EStG, Income Tax Act; for corporations Section 8a KStG, Corporation Tax Act). If net interest expense, that is, interest expense minus interest income, amounts to €3 million or more (exemption threshold, Freigrenze), it is deductible only up to 30% of taxable EBITDA. The non-deductible part is carried forward to later years as an interest carryforward, so that part of the assumed tax advantage is deferred or lost altogether.

A valuation that ends with a point estimate claims a precision that it cannot have with estimated inputs. The result of a DCF is a range, and its width is information too. A narrow range shows that the business is predictable. If the range is twice as wide as the share price, no useful statement about the value can be derived from the model. The result should therefore be rounded to ten cents or to half euros. Further decimal places from the spreadsheet arise only from the division and contain no information.

## Growth without reinvestment

The second-largest lever lies in a change that looks harmless. The perpetual growth rate is raised, but investment stays unchanged. Mathematically, the additional growth then arises without any capital being deployed for it. A company that grows at 3% permanently and earns 12% on the capital employed must reinvest a quarter of its profit. In the starting case with lower growth, an eighth is enough.

bloecke.titel: Perpetual growth, reinvestment and enterprise value (illustrative calculation with NOPAT €100 million, ROIC 12%, WACC 8.5%)

bloecke.md: The relationship g = ROIC × reinvestment rate applies. If g is raised, either the cash flow must therefore fall or a higher return on capital must be justified. In the model, the correctly calculated increase from 1.5% to 3.0% adds 9.1% of value, whereas the increase without an adjusted reinvestment rate adds 27.3%. The difference of around 18 percentage points is phantom value, created solely because one line was not changed along with the rest.

## Upper limit for the perpetual growth rate

The perpetual growth rate covers all years after the forecast horizon, which account for most of the value. If it is above long-term nominal economic growth, the company's share of the economy mathematically keeps growing until at some point it owns everything. A practical upper limit is the yield on long-term government bonds, because it already contains an expectation of inflation and real growth. On 18 September 2026, the yield on ten-year German federal bonds was around 3.5%. The bond yield is only a guide. With 4.5% perpetual growth, however, the valuer must be able to justify why this particular company should grow permanently faster than the country in which it sells its products.

The same check also works in reverse for an exit multiple, from which the implied g can be backed out. If this g does not fit the growth assumption of the explicit forecast period, the two parts of the model contradict each other.

## Choosing the earnings base

Cyclical companies look cheap precisely when their earnings are at their peak. Their low P/E ratio in this phase results from the high earnings in the denominator and not from a low share price. The gap between two metrics for the same market shows how large this effect can become. On 18 September 2026, the trailing P/E of the S&P 500 was 26.07 and the cyclically adjusted Shiller CAPE 40.94. Current earnings are therefore, as an approximation, a good half above their inflation-adjusted ten-year average.

Normalised earnings, that is, averages over a full cycle instead of the figures for the most recent year, help against this error. Another option is owner earnings, which Buffett defined in 1986 in the appendix to the Berkshire annual report. They are reported earnings plus non-cash charges minus the average annual maintenance expenditure. The difference from free cash flow lies in this average. Otherwise, a single year without investment produces a cash flow yield that will not recur.

## Share count and dilution

The last step divides by the number of shares, which is tacitly treated as constant even though it changes. Under IFRS 2, share-based payment must be recognised as an expense at fair value. It is non-cash, but it still reduces the economic share of existing shareholders. The diluted share count, which IAS 33 requires to be disclosed alongside the basic count, therefore belongs in the calculation. What matters is how it develops over several years.

bloecke.titel: Value per share with an unchanged equity value of €800 million (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: The value of the company is the same in every year; only the number of shares rises.

bloecke.md:
At 2.5% dilution a year, the value per share falls by 21.9% over ten years, even though the value of the company stays the same. Share buybacks can offset this effect. In that case, they serve to pay for the compensation. Counting them at the same time as a return of capital to shareholders and treating the compensation as a free incentive is double counting.

## Order of result and assumptions

The most dangerous error is the wrong order. The desired result is fixed first, and the assumptions that lead to it are chosen afterwards. This variant is hard to spot because every single assumption remains justifiable. Two patterns point to it. In the first pattern, costs are only ever adjusted downwards. Special items that occur in each of the last five years, however, are part of ongoing costs. That is why the ESMA guidelines on alternative performance measures have required a reconciliation to the IFRS figure since 3 July 2016. For financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027, IFRS 18 makes such measures subject to systematic disclosure for the first time. In the second pattern, your own purchase price comes up in the discussion even though it does not appear in any valuation input, neither in the cash flow nor in the denominator nor in the bridge.

“I'll wait until I'm back to break-even” refers to a past decision and says nothing about the value. The market does not know your purchase price. As a test, consider whether you would open the position afresh today at this price. If the answer differs from the decision to hold, the anchor rather than the model is determining what you do.

bloecke.titel: Sources of error in the course of a valuation
bloecke.unter: Each step of the valuation has a typical error. Errors in early steps carry over into all later ones, and in the model the bridge to equity amplifies them by a factor of 1.56.

schritte.titel: Write down the assumptions before the result
schritte.text: Record the earnings base, growth, reinvestment rate, WACC, bridge items and share count with date and rationale before the formula is calculated.
Check whether the reinvestment rate fits g and ROIC, whether g is below nominal economic growth and whether the exit multiple implies the same g.
Take net financial debt, pensions, minorities and non-operating assets into account, and only then divide by the diluted share count.

schritte.titel: Report a range instead of a point estimate
schritte.text: Vary at least the WACC and g, and round the result to a sensible number of digits. Put the share price alongside for comparison, but do not include it in the calculation.
Determine what growth the current share price implies. If your own assumption is more favourable than the market's, you must be able to name a reason for it.

bloecke.md: If, a year later, you place the actual figures next to the original assumptions in the old valuation file, the direction of your own errors becomes visible. Usually the margin and growth assumptions were too optimistic and capital expenditure was set too low. For most valuers, this direction is stable and can therefore be factored in as a flat-rate discount.

mitnehmen: The bridge from enterprise value to equity value amplifies every error; in the model, an enterprise value that is 20% too high leads to a value per share that is 31% too high.
Growth requires capital; if g is raised without a matching reinvestment rate, phantom value arises, in the model 18 percentage points purely from one line that was not changed.
The perpetual growth rate must not exceed long-term nominal economic growth; the yield on long-term government bonds is a useful upper limit.
The share count changes over time; 2.5% dilution a year lowers the value per share by just under 22% over ten years without anything changing at the company.
A point estimate with two decimal places suggests a precision the model does not have; what makes sense is a range whose calculation does not include the purchase price.

begriffe.text: The impression of accuracy that arises when a model turns estimated inputs into a point estimate with decimal places. Computational precision says nothing about the quality of the assumptions.
Reconciliation from enterprise value to the value of equity. Net financial debt, pension provisions and non-controlling interests are deducted, and non-operating assets are added.

Share of operating profit after tax that stays in the company to finance growth. The relationship is g = ROIC × reinvestment rate. A growth assumption without a matching reinvestment rate is unfunded.
Earnings averaged over a full business cycle. They prevent a cyclical company from looking cheap at the earnings peak because of a superficially low multiple.
Number of shares including all rights that can lead to new shares, for example from share-based payment or convertible bonds. IAS 33 requires it to be disclosed alongside the basic number.
